item.title: J.P. Morgan: US humanoid production could reach 300,000–400,000 units by 2030 and 1.5 million by 2035, with hands and actuators the binding constraint
item.description: The bank's first full US humanoid forecast puts near-term value in component suppliers, not robot makers, and names the four bottlenecks it expects to hold the industry back.
item.content:encoded:
The bank's first full US humanoid forecast puts near-term value in component suppliers, not robot makers, and names the four bottlenecks it expects to hold the industry back.

J.P. Morgan analysts told clients on Thursday that US production of humanoid robots could reach 300,000 to 400,000 units a year by 2030 and roughly 1.5 million by 2035, according to a Reuters report of the note. Outside Tesla, the bank says most US makers are targeting annual output of 10,000 to 30,000 units each. It sizes the component market for actuators, motors and vision systems at close to $30 billion by 2035.

What the numbers assume

The forecast rests on three claims. Labour shortages in manufacturing, logistics and warehousing are persistent. Robot costs are approaching parity with the labour they replace, with the bank estimating about $100,000 a year in savings per customer from running robots across multiple shifts. And production capacity is being built, with Tesla's Optimus, Agility's Digit, Boston Dynamics' Atlas, Figure and Apptronik's Apollo all moving from demonstrations toward commercial deployment. Agility's Nasdaq debut on November 9 gave the sector its first pure-play public comparable, so this note arrives as investors are looking for a framework.

For scale, 400,000 units a year by 2030 would be roughly the number of industrial robots installed worldwide in a strong year today, concentrated in one country and one form factor. It is a bull case, and the bank says so by listing what could stop it.

The four bottlenecks

J.P. Morgan describes near-term progress as "supply constrained, with a few binding bottlenecks: hands, actuators, the brain, and production capacity." Hands are the hardest mechanical problem in the field; dexterous, durable, affordable hands do not yet exist at volume. Actuators and harmonic drives are a supply-chain question, which is why the bank's favoured names are suppliers: Timken, Robotis, Leader Harmonious Drive Systems, Orbbec and Cognex. The brain is a training-data and compute problem; every humanoid company is now also a simulation company, which is what Skild AI's open-sourced Steel solver and Nvidia's GR00T 2 release this week were about. Production capacity is the slowest to fix and the most exposed to policy.

On policy, the note points to the Trump administration's finding that imported robotics and industrial machinery pose a national-security risk, which could lead to tariffs or other measures favouring domestic production. That cuts both ways for the forecast: it protects US makers from Chinese competition at the same time as it raises the cost of the Chinese actuators many of them use.

The counter-argument

Humanoid forecasts have a poor record. Deployed units today number in the hundreds to low thousands, mostly in pilots with the makers' own investors as customers. The $100,000 savings figure assumes multi-shift reliability that no vendor has demonstrated at fleet scale, and it assumes the task is one a humanoid does better than a wheeled or fixed robot, a question Boston Dynamics itself raised by testing a wheeled Atlas. Component suppliers also face the risk that the winners vertically integrate, as Tesla has said it will.

What to watch

Agility's first quarterly report as a public company, which will give the first audited unit and revenue figures in the sector; whether any maker publishes fleet uptime; the administration's robotics tariff decision; and J.P. Morgan's component-supplier names, which will now be bid on the thesis before a single 2030 unit ships.

item.title: Skild AI's Steel runs robot simulation up to 13x faster than PhysX on mixed batches and uses 62% less memory; here is what the numbers cover
item.description: A $14 billion startup contributed its rigid-body solver to Nvidia's open-source Newton engine a week after Nvidia shipped Isaac Lab 3.0; the benchmark is real, the headline multiple needs context, and the licence is not stated.
item.content:encoded:
A $14 billion startup contributed its rigid-body solver to Nvidia's open-source Newton engine a week after Nvidia shipped Isaac Lab 3.0; the benchmark is real, the headline multiple needs context, and the licence is not stated.

Skild AI released Steel on November 9, a GPU rigid-body dynamics solver it built with Nvidia and is contributing to Newton, the open-source physics engine Nvidia launched for robot learning. The name stands for Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning. It ships inside Newton as newton.solvers.SolverSteel, shares Newton's model representation and collision code, and is meant to drop into Isaac Lab, Nvidia's training framework, which reached version 3.0 at the Conference on Robot Learning a week ago.

Skild is not a small contributor. It raised about $1.4 billion in January at a valuation above $14 billion, led by SoftBank with Nvidia's venture arm, Bezos Expeditions, Samsung, LG and Salesforce among the backers, and sells the Skild Brain, a foundation model meant to control many robot bodies without per-robot retraining. Steel is the simulation engine behind that model's training.

What was measured

All benchmarks ran on one Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU and measure simulation throughput, not end-to-end training speed. On a suite of 20 single-task Isaac Lab environments, with each engine at its best batch size, Steel's geometric-mean speed-up over PhysX was 3.8x, and it was faster on 19 of the 20 tasks. MuJoCo Warp, Google DeepMind's GPU engine, was 2.9x PhysX on the same suite, so Steel's lead over it is about 1.3x. On the hardest single task, a Kuka arm with an Allegro hand lifting an object, Steel was 6.7x PhysX.

The larger multiples come from heterogeneous batches, where one simulation holds 5, 10, 15 or 20 different task types at once. There Steel reached 9.2x to 13x PhysX at peak, hitting 3.9 million environment steps per second across 245,760 environments with 20 task types. At a matched batch of 61,440 environments, Steel ran 3.61 million steps per second against 300,000 for PhysX, a 12x gap, while using about 11 GiB of GPU memory against 29 GiB, roughly 62% less. Skild notes the PhysX comparison used Isaac Sim 6.1.0 and that the earlier 6.0.0 release ran some mixtures up to 2.7x faster, which narrows the gap for anyone on the older build.

Steel combines reduced-coordinate articulation dynamics with projected Gauss-Seidel constraint solving, handles rigid-to-deformable coupling for cables, cloth and granular material, supports compliant and hydroelastic contact, and puts settled bodies to sleep to skip most of the solve work. An opt-in differentiable step lets Newton's tape back-propagate through the solver; Skild shows drone model-predictive control and a trajectory optimisation using an experimental smooth-contact model.

Why heterogeneous batches matter

A single-task simulation is how most robot learning papers have been done. A foundation model that must learn locomotion, manipulation and navigation across many bodies is trained on a mixture, and PhysX's design, tuned for games and single scenes, handles that case badly. That is why Skild's best numbers are there and why they are not an unfair comparison for Skild's own purpose; they are simply not the number to quote if you train one policy on one task.

The counter-argument

The benchmark conditions are published, which is better than most of the field, but they were chosen by the vendor, on a Newton release candidate, against a PhysX build the vendor acknowledges was not the fastest available. Throughput is not sample efficiency: a faster simulator that produces the same gradients saves money, not training steps. The blog post also does not name a licence, which for an open-source contribution to an open-source engine is an unusual omission; the GitHub repository is the place to check before any commercial use. And Skild's incentive is clear: a faster Newton makes the Nvidia ecosystem, in which it has raised and spent billions, more attractive relative to MuJoCo and Genesis.

What to watch

Nvidia's own adoption of Steel as a default in Isaac Lab; MuJoCo Warp's response, since the 1.3x gap is within a release; independent reproductions on H100 and consumer GPUs, where memory savings matter more; whether the licence is permissive; and whether Skild publishes sim-to-real results showing policies trained on Steel transfer as well as PhysX-trained ones, which is the only number that determines whether the speed is worth anything.

item.title: Nvidia's GR00T 2 claims 71% one-shot success on 50 tasks. Here is what that number does and does not say
item.description: A new open world-action model trained on 100,000 hours of human video, a simulator that agents can configure themselves, and a benchmark claim that needs the task list before anyone builds a business case on it.
item.content:encoded:
A new open world-action model trained on 100,000 hours of human video, a simulator that agents can configure themselves, and a benchmark claim that needs the task list before anyone builds a business case on it.

Nvidia used the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin on November 9 to introduce GR00T 2, which it describes as an open frontier world action model built on its Cosmos platform, alongside Isaac Lab 3.0, a major revision of its robot-training simulator. The announcements came with partner names from Bosch and Siemens to Skild AI, Dyna Robotics and FieldAI, and with a set of benchmark numbers that deserve a careful read.

What was announced

GR00T 2 is trained on robot demonstrations and on human data, including 100,000 hours of open-source egocentric video that Nvidia released earlier this year as part of its EgoHand dataset, which it says has been downloaded more than 40,000 times in two weeks. Nvidia says the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without any task-specific demonstration, averaged 71% success across those 50 tasks when given one demonstration per task, and reached 95% with five. It also says GR00T 2 ranks in the top three on four public suites: RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces.

Isaac Lab 3.0 lets agents set up training environments from simulation-ready assets, switch between the PhysX and Newton physics engines, choose renderers for perception training, and use a new reinforcement post-training library for models like GR00T. Newton adds deformable objects such as cables and cloth and articulated multi-joint hands. Nvidia claims up to 2.5 times the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 on a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark. A result called AlphaNIST, built in Isaac Lab, trained a single policy to all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board at over 98% training success, against 81% for separate per-task policies, using roughly 39 times less GPU time.

Reading the numbers

The 71% and 95% figures are Nvidia's own, and the announcement does not name the 50 tasks, the robots used, or how many rollouts sit behind each average. 'Completed at least once' is a generous bar: a task that succeeds in one attempt out of twenty counts. Averages can also hide tasks that never succeed. Nvidia's own RoboLab team has published the uncertainty maths: a 90% rate measured over 70 rollouts has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 80% to 96%. And 95% with five demonstrations is a few-shot result, not the zero-shot generality the phrase 'frontier world action model' suggests.

Independent suites tell a humbler story. The RoboDojo paper reports a best real-world score of 12.8% for the strongest model tested against 100% for human experts, and the Stanford AI Index has highlighted the gap between near-90% scores on RLBench and around 12% full-task success on BEHAVIOR-1K. Those suites differ from Nvidia's, so this is not a contradiction, but it shows how much task design drives the headline figure. Licence terms matter too: the previous checkpoint, GR00T N1.6, shipped under an Nvidia licence whose text is titled non-commercial, and GR00T 2's terms and weights release date were not stated.

Why it still matters

The strategic move is not the model but the stack. If every serious robot developer trains in Isaac Lab, evaluates in Isaac Lab-Arena, and starts from a GR00T checkpoint, Nvidia owns the toolchain of embodied AI the way CUDA owns model training. That is why the partner list is the most informative part of the announcement, and why Agility, Figure and the other humanoid companies now going public will be asked by investors how much of their stack is Nvidia's.

What to watch

The GR00T 2 licence and weights release, slated for around year end. Publication of the 50-task suite and rollout counts. Independent results on RoboDojo and RoboCasa365 once outside labs run the model. And whether AlphaNIST's single-policy assembly result reproduces on physical hardware, which is the claim a factory buyer can actually use.

item.title: Agility Robotics is the first public humanoid company. Its numbers explain why that is hard
item.description: $174,000 of revenue, a $362 million half-year loss and $300 million of orders for a robot that ships in 2027: AGLT is a bet on throughput targets nobody outside the company has seen. Axon's $1.2 billion Skydio deal shows the other route.
item.content:encoded:
$174,000 of revenue, a $362 million half-year loss and $300 million of orders for a robot that ships in 2027: AGLT is a bet on throughput targets nobody outside the company has seen. Axon's $1.2 billion Skydio deal shows the other route.

Agility Robotics started trading on Nasdaq on November 5 under the ticker AGLT, after completing its merger with the blank-cheque company Churchill Capital Corp XI. It is the first company whose business is humanoid robots to list on a US exchange, and it did so without a bell-ringing ceremony and with a prospectus that reads more like a hardware startup's Series C deck than a public-company filing.

The numbers

The company raised about $465 million in gross proceeds: $201 million from a private placement led by Foxconn, $164 million from the SPAC trust and $100 million raised after the deal was announced. Nvidia is an investor. Against that, Agility reported $174,000 of revenue in the first six months of 2026, mostly from related parties, and a loss of $362 million over the same period. Management says the raise covers current needs but not self-sustaining operations.

The investment case rests on what comes next. Agility says it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders from roughly 30 customers for Digit 5, its next-generation robot, subject to contractual milestones, features and specifications. Digit 5 has not been publicly demonstrated. Prototypes are due at CES in January 2027, early access in the first half of 2027 and general availability at the end of 2027.

What Digit does today

The current Digit is working at nine customers, including GXO, Schaeffler, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and Mercado Libre. At a GXO site in Georgia it has moved more than 100,000 totes, and GXO plans two more US facilities in early 2027. AGCO has signed a pilot in Kansas, and three unnamed manufacturers, a global automaker, an automotive-components company and a consumer-products maker, are in paid programmes. Agility's RoboFab plant in Salem, Oregon, is designed for up to 10,000 robots a year.

The robot handles heavy, repetitive tote moves with about 98% placement accuracy but cannot yet do complex manipulation. The commercial pitch is roughly $100,000 of annual savings per robot, which only works if the robot runs long enough between charges and maintenance to replace a meaningful fraction of a shift. Those are the variables the order milestones will test.

Axon's alternative: buy the distribution

A day later, Axon, the Taser and body-camera company, said it would invest a further $1.2 billion in drone maker Skydio in cash and stock, at a $5.2 billion pre-money valuation, lifting its fully diluted stake by about 20 percentage points. Axon becomes Skydio's exclusive public-safety distributor in the US and Canada. Skydio says it has more than 1,500 public-safety customers and expects about $1 billion of bookings this fiscal year; Axon puts the drone-as-first-responder market at about $13 billion. The transactions close across the fourth quarter and the first quarter of 2027.

The contrast with Agility is instructive. Skydio is a physical-AI company with a thousand-plus paying customers and a channel partner that already sells to every police department in North America; it stayed private and took strategic capital. Agility has nine customers and a 2027 product, and went public through a SPAC. One is monetising deployment; the other is financing it.

The counter-argument

Humanoid bulls will say revenue is the wrong metric for a company whose factory is built and whose order book is ten times the capital it just raised on a per-year basis. If Digit 5 hits its targets, Agility will have a public currency to scale with while private rivals such as Figure, 1X and Apptronik are still raising. The bear case is simply that the targets are unpublished and the burn is $60 million a month.

What to watch

The first 10-Q, which will put the milestone conditions in a public filing. CES in January for Digit 5. GXO's two additional sites, which would be the first evidence of repeat deployment at scale. And how AGLT trades through its lock-up, because every private humanoid round for the next year will be marked against it.

item.title: Physicl raises $10M to make simulations real enough to train robots, as humanoid funding hits a record
item.description: The bottleneck in robotics is no longer the model or the hardware. It is believable practice environments, and a new wave of startups is selling exactly that.
item.content:encoded:
The bottleneck in robotics is no longer the model or the hardware. It is believable practice environments, and a new wave of startups is selling exactly that.

Physicl, a startup building high-fidelity simulated environments for training robots, has raised $10 million, TechCrunch reported on November 6. The pitch is simple: robots learn by practising, practising in the physical world is slow and expensive, and today's simulators are not realistic enough for skills learned there to survive contact with reality. Make the digital world "real enough" and you can train millions of hours overnight.

Why simulation is the bottleneck

Language models had the internet to learn from. Robots have nothing comparable: there is no trillion-token archive of a hand picking up a cup. The industry's answer is to manufacture experience, either by teleoperating real robots and recording them, or by simulating. Simulation scales, but the gap between simulated and real physics (friction, deformable objects, lighting, sensor noise) has historically wasted much of what was learned. Closing that gap is now a product category, and Physicl is one of several companies selling into it alongside the simulation stacks offered by the large chip and cloud vendors.

The money around it

The context is a funding boom. Dealroom's tracker put venture investment in humanoid robotics at $8.7 billion for 2026 by late July, already an all-time high, and noted that China accounts for roughly two-thirds of that total, with the US share down to about 15%. Earlier in the year Apptronik's $520 million round pushed its total raised to nearly $1 billion.

Deployments are following the money, cautiously. In October, agricultural-equipment maker AGCO announced a pilot of Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid at its Hesston, Kansas plant, and Agility signed a safety partnership covering its newest robot. The pattern across announcements is narrow tasks, defined zones and a safety vendor in the loop.

What to watch

  • Sim-to-real benchmarks. Expect simulation vendors to publish transfer rates (how much a sim-trained skill degrades in the real world) the way model labs publish benchmarks.
  • Who owns the environments. The large platforms are bundling simulation with chips and cloud; independents like Physicl bet that fidelity wins over bundling.
  • The China gap. Two-thirds of humanoid capital is now there. Western policy on robotics exports and supply chains is the next place this shows up.
